questions.q: What problem does normalization primarily solve?
options: Slow reads caused by too many indexes on one table
Storage exhaustion from keeping large binary files in rows
Queries failing because column types are inconsistent
Update anomalies from the same fact stored in multiple places
questions.explanation: Normalization stores each fact exactly once, so an update touches one row and copies cannot drift out of sync. Its goal is consistency, not read speed.

questions.q: How is a many-to-many relationship modeled in a relational schema?
options: A junction table holding foreign keys to both related tables
A comma-separated list of IDs in a text column
Duplicated rows in both of the tables, one copy per relationship pair
A nullable foreign key on whichever table is larger
questions.explanation: A junction (join) table gives each pairing its own row, keeping both sides indexable and referentially intact. Comma-separated ID lists cannot be constrained or joined efficiently.

questions.q: What makes a good primary key?
options: A value users recognize, like an email address
A stable, unique, compact value that never needs to change
The row's creation timestamp captured at full millisecond precision
A hash of all the row's columns concatenated
questions.explanation: Every foreign key copies the primary key, so it must be unique and never change; compactness keeps indexes small. Business-meaningful values fail the stability test.

questions.q: Why choose a surrogate key (auto-ID) over a natural key like email?
options: Surrogate integer keys compress better inside backups and archives
Natural keys cannot be indexed efficiently by B-trees
Natural attributes change; a surrogate stays stable across those changes
Surrogate keys are required by the SQL standard
questions.explanation: A user can change their email, which would cascade through every referencing table. A meaningless surrogate has no business reason to ever change.

questions.q: What does a foreign key constraint actually enforce?
options: Referenced rows must exist, blocking orphaned references
Both tables must physically reside on the same disk volume together
Joins between the two tables will always use an index
The referencing column is automatically made unique
questions.explanation: Referential integrity means the database rejects inserts pointing at missing parents and blocks or cascades deletes that would orphan children. It says nothing about uniqueness or storage.

questions.q: What is denormalization?
options: Removing all constraints so writes never fail
Splitting wide tables into many narrower ones to improve cache efficiency
Converting a relational schema to a document schema
Deliberately duplicating data to make specific reads cheaper
questions.explanation: Denormalization intentionally copies data to avoid joins or aggregations on hot read paths, accepting extra write work and the risk of drift as the price.

questions.q: A soft delete marks rows with deleted_at instead of removing them. What is the main operational catch?
options: Storage grows without bound and the space can never be reclaimed afterward
Foreign keys stop working on soft-deleted rows
Every query must remember to filter deleted rows, or leaks occur
Soft-deleted rows lock their pages until purged
questions.explanation: The rows remain fully visible to any query lacking the deleted_at IS NULL predicate, so one forgotten filter resurrects deleted data. Views or query-scope defaults mitigate this.

questions.q: Third normal form (3NF) mainly eliminates what?
options: Repeating groups of similar columns packed inside a single row
Non-key columns depending on other non-key columns
Multi-valued dependencies between candidate keys
Composite keys with more than two columns
questions.explanation: 3NF removes transitive dependencies: every non-key attribute must depend on the key directly, not through another non-key column such as zip determining city.

questions.q: An orders table stores product price at purchase time, though products has price. Why is this duplication correct?
options: Order history must reflect the price paid, even after the catalog price changes
It saves one join, which is always worth the storage
Product prices cannot be indexed for historical queries
A foreign key into products would lock the entire catalog during each checkout
questions.explanation: The price paid is a distinct historical fact, not a copy of the current catalog price. Joining to products would silently rewrite past invoices whenever pricing changed.

questions.q: Your users table has 40 mostly-NULL columns like 'fax_number2'. What schema smell is this?
options: Excessive normalization that splits the data into overly fine pieces
A god table accreting unrelated optional attributes over time
Index bloat from over-indexing sparse columns
Improper sharding of a wide-column store
questions.explanation: Sparse, unrelated columns signal that several distinct concepts were bolted onto one table. Extracting them into related tables or a JSON attributes column restores coherence.

questions.q: Why does the entity-attribute-value (EAV) pattern usually backfire?
options: Attribute names inevitably collide across entity types, silently corrupting stored data
EAV tables cannot be backed up consistently
Databases limit tables to 1,000 rows of metadata
Simple queries become sprawling self-joins, and types and constraints go unenforced
questions.explanation: EAV pushes schema into data, so each attribute needs another self-join and the engine can no longer enforce types, NOT NULL, or foreign keys. Query plans degrade badly.

questions.q: A migration must add a NOT NULL column (no static default fits) to a 500M-row hot table. Safe approach?
options: Add it NOT NULL immediately; the database will backfill the value automatically
Schedule a full maintenance window, because large schema changes always require downtime
Add it nullable, backfill in batches, then enforce NOT NULL once every row is set
Copy into a new table and swap a view over the top in one step
questions.explanation: Nullable adds are cheap metadata changes; batched backfills avoid one giant long-held lock and huge transactions. The constraint is validated only after all rows are populated.

questions.q: Comments belong to posts, and a post renders with its latest 3 comments. What is the standard relational model?
options: A comments array column on posts, updated by trigger
A comments table with a post_id foreign key, joined with ORDER BY and LIMIT
A physically separate database for comments, isolating their write load from posts
Copying the latest three comments into the posts row
questions.explanation: A one-to-many foreign key with an index on (post_id, created_at) serves the top-3 query cheaply while keeping comments independently queryable, editable, and paginable.

questions.q: Why do append-only (event-sourced) schemas store immutable events instead of updating rows in place?
options: Full history is preserved, and state can be rebuilt or audited at any past point
Append operations are the only writes that SQL guarantees to be fully atomic
Immutable rows compress to zero bytes after archival
Updates are forbidden once a table has a clustered index
questions.explanation: In-place updates destroy the prior value; an event log keeps every transition, so current state is a replay and any historical state or audit trail remains reconstructable.

questions.q: A status column holds 'active', 'actve', 'ACTIVE' across rows. Which design would have prevented this?
options: Storing the status as a small integer with its meanings documented in the team wiki
A trigger that lowercases all text columns on insert
A constrained type: enum, CHECK constraint, or lookup table with a foreign key
Weekly data-quality jobs that fix drifted values
questions.explanation: Only the database rejecting invalid values at write time prevents drift. Cleanup jobs and conventions repair damage after the fact; a constraint makes bad data impossible.

questions.q: When is denormalizing a read-heavy aggregate (like post like_counts) into a column justified?
options: Whenever any query is slower than 100 ms
Only inside document databases, since relational engines forbid such duplication
Whenever the underlying count is written far more often than it is ever read
When counting on demand is too costly and slightly stale counts are acceptable
questions.explanation: A cached counter trades exactness and extra write cost for cheap reads, so it pays off precisely when reads dominate and approximate freshness is tolerable.

questions.q: Multi-tenant SaaS: single shared tables with tenant_id versus schema-per-tenant. What chiefly argues for shared tables at 50k tenants?
options: Shared tables encrypt each tenant's rows separately by default
Per-tenant schemas give better cache utilization at scale
Migrations and connection pooling stay manageable; 50k schemas overwhelm tooling and catalogs
Shared tables make noisy-neighbor isolation automatic
questions.explanation: One shared schema means one migration and one pool. Fifty thousand schemas multiply every DDL change by 50k and bloat catalog metadata past what most tooling handles.

questions.q: You must rename a heavily-used column with zero downtime. Standard multi-step pattern?
options: Rename it inside one transaction; the lock makes the change invisible to all clients
Rename in the ORM only, keeping the database column forever
Announce a maintenance window and rename during low traffic
Add new column, dual-write, backfill, migrate readers, then drop the old one
questions.explanation: The expand-migrate-contract sequence keeps both names valid while old and new code run together, so no deploy ordering can break. An atomic rename breaks in-flight clients instantly.

questions.q: An audit requirement demands provable knowledge of a row's state on any past date. Which schema approach fits?
options: Nightly full-table dumps retained for ninety days
Temporal (system-versioned) tables recording validity ranges per row version
A last_modified timestamp column on every table
The database write-ahead log at its default retention, replayed whenever auditors ask
questions.explanation: System-versioned tables keep every row version with valid-from/valid-to bounds, so an as-of query returns the exact state at any instant. Snapshots and last_modified lose intermediate changes.

questions.q: Your M2M junction table (user_id, group_id) now needs 'role within group' and 'joined date'. Correct evolution?
options: Add them as columns on the junction table, which models the membership itself
Create one additional junction table for each newly required membership attribute
Move role and date onto the users table as arrays
Denormalize memberships into a JSON column on groups
questions.explanation: The junction row is the membership entity, so attributes of that relationship belong on it. Role and joined date depend on the (user, group) pair, not on either side alone.
